newsitem.title: USA: CME to lift currency dual-trading curb for 90 days.
newsitem.headline: CME to lift currency dual-trading curb for 90 days.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange board approved a plan that would nearly reverse a self-imposed rule that has curbed dual trading in its busiest currency futures since 1991, the exchange said Wednesday.

If futures regulators approve, the three-month plan passed at Tuesday's board meeting would let members trade both for themselves and for their customers in the mark, yen and Swiss franc futures pits for most of the regular trading day.
No starting date has been set yet for the trial program, which further softens CME's once-adamant stance against the controversial pit practice.
The program would keep the curb in place from the 0720 CDT/1220 GMT opening until 0745 CDT/1245 GMT, thus covering the release of most major U.S. economic reports.
Dual trading also would stay restricted during the closing range each afternoon in the mark, yen and Swiss franc pits.

Still, the move represents an about-face for the CME, which voluntarily curbed dual trading in active currency futures in May 1991 after a federal probe of futures trading practices spotlighted potential trading abuses.
Other U.S. futures markets, such as the Chicago Board of Trade, chafed at CME's move and refused to curb the practice.

The CME's home-grown rule, which critics said was intended to deflect stricter federal trade-recording requirements, meant CME members no longer could fill customer orders and trade for their own accounts in the same product unless they got a written exemption from the customer.
The newest effort follows a plan CME tried in July 1995 after it got the regulatory okay to modify the trading curb.

That pilot expired without fanfare and the curb was reinstated, although CME in October 1996 eliminated in currencies a related restriction on who could stand on the coveted top step in the trading pit.
The latest plan would not affect some currency futures such as sterling, which often do not qualify for the curb that applies to contracts where daily volume averages 10,000 contracts or more.

A CME spokeswoman said the board decided to try the pilot program at the urging of currency traders on the CME's floor who are losing business to over-the-counter and exchange-for-physicals currency markets.
The CME is trying a number of plans to rescue flagging currency futures pit volume, including the all-or-none rule and the GLOBEX Foreign Exchange Facility.
